title: Instructions, Not Invaders
paragraphs: For most of the history of vaccination, protecting the body meant showing it a weakened, inactivated or partial version of a pathogen so that the immune system could learn to recognise the real thing. Messenger RNA vaccines take a less direct route. Instead of supplying the foreign protein itself, they deliver genetic instructions, wrapped in tiny fatty particles, that prompt the recipient's own cells to manufacture a harmless fragment of it for a short time. In the case of the COVID-19 vaccines, that fragment was the spike protein found on the surface of the coronavirus.

A persistent worry is that such instructions might rewrite a person's genes. According to the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, however, the messenger molecule never enters the nucleus, where DNA is kept, and cells break it down after the protein has been made. The instructions, in other words, are read and then discarded rather than stored.

The technology also appeared, to many observers, to have emerged from nowhere. In reality it rested on decades of slow and frequently unfashionable laboratory work. One early obstacle was that synthetic messenger RNA tended to provoke inflammation, which made it unsuitable for use in people. Katalin Kariko and Drew Weissman showed that chemically modifying certain building blocks of the molecule largely dampened that reaction, a discovery for which they shared the 2023 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine.

When the pandemic arrived, this groundwork allowed vaccines to be developed at an unprecedented pace, and one of the first received emergency authorisation in the United States in December 2020. The speed reflected years of accumulated knowledge, not the omission of safety testing: the authorisation followed a review of data from a large clinical trial. Whether the same approach can be extended to other diseases, including some cancers, remains an open question for researchers.
